meters.label: Classes to read for one run

frames.narration: One class, PayrollReport, calculates pay, formats the file and saves it. Finance, operations and IT each depend on a different part of it, so three teams share one class.
Finance changes a tax rule. The developer edits the one class and has to re-verify all six behaviours, because nothing separates the tax code from the layout and storage code next to it.
The tax edit shifts a column, and operations finds the report layout broken. A change that one team asked for has broken something another team relies on. That is the cost the principle is about.

The team splits by reason to change: PayCalculator for finance, ReportFormatter for operations, ReportStore for IT, and a thin coordinator. Overtime, tax and bonus stay together, because they change together.
Now a tax change edits only PayCalculator. No code from operations or IT is in the edited class, and only 4 behaviours need to be checked again, down from 6.
Someone reads the principle as one method per class and splits further: rules, rate tables and calculators, header and row formatters, path resolvers and serializers. The design now has 16 classes.

The same tax change now edits TaxCalculator, TaxRule and TaxBracketTable. Nothing else is at risk, but one reason to change has been spread over three files, and following a report run means reading 16 classes.
The sweet spot is the middle design: one class per actor. Splitting further adds reading and editing cost without removing any risk, and merging back would put three teams in one class again.
